**Title:** A Department in Turmoil: The Confirmation of Michael Mukasey and the Debate over Executive Power

In the late summer of 2007, the United States Department of Justice found itself in the throes of one of the most severe institutional crises in its modern history. Following months of damaging scandals—most notably the controversial firing of several U.S. Attorneys and allegations of rampant politicization within the agency—Attorney General Alberto Gonzales resigned. His departure left a demoralized, leaderless, and adrift Department of Justice (DOJ) during a critical juncture in the post-9/11 era. Seeking to restore credibility and steady the floating ship, President George W. Bush turned to Michael B. Mukasey, a highly respected retired federal judge from the Southern District of New York with extensive national security experience, nominating him as the nation’s 81st Attorney General.

While Mukasey initially appeared to be a consensus candidate capable of bridging the partisan divide, his confirmation process quickly ran aground on one of the defining moral and legal issues of the post-9/11 Bush presidency: the use of "enhanced interrogation techniques," specifically waterboarding. 

During his confirmation hearings before the Senate Judiciary Committee, lawmakers pressed Mukasey to explicitly declare waterboarding—a practice that simulates drowning—to be illegal under federal law and international anti-torture statutes. Mukasey resisted, taking a nuanced but contentious legal stance. He argued that because he was not currently privy to the classified operational details of the CIA’s interrogation program, he could not definitively categorize the practice as torture. Furthermore, he expressed concern that declaring the technique illegal retroactively could expose intelligence officers who had acted in good faith under existing executive legal opinions to severe legal liability.

Mukasey’s refusal to outright condemn waterboarding transformed what was expected to be a smooth confirmation into a fierce political battle. Civil liberties advocates and prominent Democrats, including Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy, argued that an Attorney General must be willing to state unequivocally that waterboarding is torture, viewing Mukasey’s hedge as an unacceptable defense of executive overreach. 

Despite the intense opposition, Mukasey’s candidacy survived due to a pragmatic calculation by a handful of key moderate Democrats. Senators such as Charles Schumer and Dianne Feinstein, while expressing disappointment over his stance on interrogation, ultimately concluded that the Department of Justice could no longer afford to remain without a confirmed leader. They believed Mukasey possessed the personal integrity and legal independence necessary to insulate the DOJ from further political interference.

On November 8, 2007, the full Senate confirmed Mukasey in a 53–40 vote—one of the narrowest margins for an Attorney General nominee in decades. Though the vote reflected a deep national fracture over executive power and human rights, Mukasey’s arrival marked a critical turning point for the Justice Department. Taking office in the final year of the Bush administration, he moved quickly to restore internal morale, re-establish traditional norms of prosecutorial independence, and provide the rudderless agency with the steady, experienced leadership needed to set it back on course.

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy (D-Vt.), who voted against the confirmation, criticized Mukasey for failing to draw a clear legal line. 

"Waterboarding has been recognized as illegal torture for generations—by American military courts, by our courts-martial, and by international tribunals," Leahy said on the Senate floor prior to the vote. "An Attorney General must be willing to tell the President that no one, not even the President, is above the law."

The issue split the Democratic caucus and turned the nomination into a national debate over the moral and legal boundaries of the Bush administration's "War on Terror." Several Democratic presidential candidates, including Senators Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton, and Joe Biden, returned to Washington to cast votes against Mukasey.

However, Mukasey’s nomination was rescued by a handful of key Democrats, most notably Senators Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.) and Charles Schumer (D-N.Y.). Both senators expressed deep frustration with Mukasey’s answers on waterboarding, but ultimately concluded that the Justice Department—rudderless and demoralized after Gonzales' departure—desperately required confirmed, competent leadership.

Schumer and Feinstein noted that Mukasey had provided written assurances promising to enforce any legislation Congress might pass banning waterboarding, and that he acknowledged the President could not ignore constitutional statutory prohibitions.

"Judge Mukasey is a man of integrity," Schumer said in explaining his vote. "While I disagree strongly with his stance on this crucial issue, I believe he will be an independent Attorney General who will restore professionalism to a severely damaged department."

President George W. Bush hailed the confirmation, praising Mukasey as a pragmatic and principled jurist. 

"Judge Mukasey is a man of great intellect, fairness, and integrity," President Bush said in a statement released by the White House following the vote. "He will be an outstanding leader for the Department of Justice, and he understands the vital role the department plays in protecting the American people from terrorism."

Mukasey, 66, spent 18 years as a federal judge in the Southern District of New York, including six years as chief judge. During his tenure on the bench, he presided over high-profile national security cases, including the 1996 trial of Omar Abdel-Rahman, the "Blind Sheikh," for his role in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing plot.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — The Senate voted late Thursday to confirm retired federal judge Michael Mukasey as the nation’s 81st attorney general, ending weeks of fiery political debate over executive power and the legal definition of torture.

The 53-40 vote was one of the narrowest margins for an attorney general nominee in modern history, reflecting deep partisan divisions in Capitol Hill’s battle with the Bush administration over interrogation techniques used in the war on terror.

Mukasey, 66, replaces Alberto Gonzales, who resigned in August following months of controversy surrounding the firing of U.S. attorneys and allegations that he politicized the Justice Department.

While Mukasey was initially praised by both Democrats and Republicans as an independent legal mind, his nomination nearly stalled after he refused to explicitly label "waterboarding"—a technique that simulates drowning—as illegal torture during his confirmation hearings.

### A Divisive Debate Over Waterboarding

The nomination forced a national debate on the ethics and legality of harsh interrogation tactics. According to a CNN/Opinion Research Corp. poll conducted as the Senate debated the nomination, a clear majority of the American public sided against the practice. 

The poll found that 58% of Americans considered waterboarding to be torture, while 38% said it was not. Additionally, 60% of respondents said they opposed the use of waterboarding by U.S. military and intelligence personnel, even when dealing with suspected terrorists.

That public skepticism was mirrored on the Senate floor, where Democrats expressed frustration with Mukasey’s testimony.

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont, voted against confirmation, arguing that Mukasey failed a fundamental constitutional test.

"Waterboarding is torture, plain and simple, and it is illegal under U.S. law and international law," Leahy said during floor debate. "I cannot support a nominee who refuses to say that a practice so blatantly illegal and abhorrent is, in fact, unlawful. The chief law enforcement officer of the United States must be willing to stand up for the rule of law."

### Key Democrats Break Ranks

Despite widespread Democratic opposition, Mukasey’s nomination was saved by a handful of key Democrats who broke ranks, including Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-New York. Schumer, who had originally suggested Mukasey to the White House as a consensus candidate, acknowledged his deep disappointment with Mukasey’s answers on torture, but argued that leaving the Justice Department without confirmed leadership was worse.

"I am deeply disappointed, frustrated, and angered by Judge Mukasey’s answers on waterboarding," Schumer said. "But at the end of the day, we are faced with a choice between an independent Attorney General who disagrees with us on some issues, or an acting Attorney General chosen by the White House who will be completely unvetted and unconfirmed. Judge Mukasey is a man of integrity who will stand up to the White House when it counts."

Republicans largely rallied behind Mukasey, praising his decades of judicial experience on the federal bench in New York, where he presided over high-profile terrorism cases, including the 1993 World Trade Center bombing trial.

Sen. Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania, the top Republican on the Judiciary Committee, praised Mukasey as the exact leader the Justice Department needed to move past recent scandals.

"Judge Mukasey is an exceptionally well-qualified nominee with an outstanding judicial record," Specter said. "He has shown throughout his career that he understands the separation of powers and the importance of an independent Department of Justice. He is precisely the person needed to restore confidence and morale at the Department."

### Looking Ahead

President Bush applauded the Senate’s action in a statement Thursday night, calling Mukasey "a man of strong character and intellect" who will "bring strong leadership to the Department of Justice."

Mukasey is expected to be sworn in promptly. Upon taking office, he will face the daunting task of rebuilding a Justice Department plagued by low morale, ongoing congressional investigations into executive overreach, and a lingering national debate over the limits of presidential power in wartime.

In September 2007, President George W. Bush nominated **Michael Mukasey**, a retired federal judge from New York, to replace Alberto Gonzales as Attorney General. Gonzales had resigned following mounting scandals, including the politicized firing of U.S. Attorneys and controversy over warrantless wiretapping. 

Although Mukasey initially received praise as a highly respected, non-partisan jurist, his confirmation stalled over his refusal to explicitly classify **waterboarding**—a simulated drowning technique used by the CIA on terror suspects—as illegal torture.

Despite intense opposition from civil rights groups and key Democratic leaders, Mukasey successfully navigated the Senate Judiciary Committee and the full Senate through a combination of strategic Democratic defections, institutional pragmatism, and nuanced legal assurances.

Here is a breakdown of how he managed to secure confirmation:

---

### 1. The Core Controversy: Waterboarding
During his confirmation hearings before the Senate Judiciary Committee in October 2007, Democrats pressed Mukasey on whether waterboarding constituted illegal torture under U.S. and international law. 

Mukasey called the practice "repugnant," but **refused to declare it illegal**. He argued that:
* He was not currently privy to the classified details of how the CIA executed the technique.
* Categorically declaring it illegal could unfairly expose past CIA interrogators—who had acted in good faith based on Bush administration legal memos—to legal liability or criminal prosecution.

This stance infuriated progressive Democrats, including Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy, and leading Democratic presidential candidates (including then-Senators Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton, and Joe Biden), who threatened to block his nomination.

---

### 2. Clearing the Senate Judiciary Committee (Key Defections)
The turning point came when two key Democratic members of the Judiciary Committee—**Senators Chuck Schumer (D-NY) and Dianne Feinstein (D-CA)**—decided to support him. 

Their support was critical for several reasons:
* **Schumer's Endorsement:** Schumer had originally suggested Mukasey to the Bush administration as a credible, moderate replacement for Gonzales. While disappointed by Mukasey’s waterboarding answers, Schumer argued that rejecting him would leave the Department of Justice in constitutional limbo under an unconfirmed acting chief.
* **Written Assurances:** In response to follow-up letters from the committee, Mukasey pledged in writing that if Congress passed a law explicitly banning waterboarding (such as applying Army Field Manual standards to the CIA), he would enforce it. He also assured senators he would resign if the President ordered him to ignore a constitutional law passed by Congress.
* **The "Lesser of Evils" Argument:** Schumer and Feinstein argued that the Department of Justice was severely damaged after the Gonzales era and desperately needed a confirmed, independent leader to restore moral and operational stability. They believed Bush would not nominate anyone who held a different view on interrogation techniques.

On November 6, 2007, the Judiciary Committee voted **11–8** to send Mukasey’s nomination to the full Senate, with Schumer and Feinstein joining all Republicans in favor.

---

### 3. Passing the Full Senate
Once out of committee, Democratic leadership (led by Majority Leader Harry Reid) chose not to filibuster the nomination, acknowledging that Mukasey had the votes to win a simple majority. 

On November 8, 2007, the full Senate confirmed Mukasey by a vote of **53–40**. 

* **Bipartisan Breakdown:** Mukasey received votes from all Republicans present and **six Democrats** (including Schumer, Feinstein, Mary Landrieu, Ben Nelson, Mark Pryor, and Evan Bayh, plus independent Joe Lieberman).
* **Opposition:** 39 Democrats and 1 Independent voted against him, primarily citing his stance on waterboarding and executive power as a dealbreaker.

---

### Summary of Why Mukasey Succeeded
1. **Gonzales Fatigue:** The Department of Justice was in crisis, and many lawmakers felt a functional DOJ under a respected former judge was preferable to an ongoing vacancy or a prolonged political war.
2. **Personal Credibility:** Mukasey had a decades-long reputation as an independent, tough-minded federal judge, making it hard for opponents to frame him as a partisan hack.
3. **Strategic Compromise:** By promising to enforce any future anti-waterboarding legislation passed by Congress, Mukasey gave moderate Democrats enough legal cover to justify voting for him.

---

### The Catalyst: Testimony and the Waterboarding Question

The nomination derailed during Mukasey’s confirmation hearings before the Senate Judiciary Committee in October 2007. Democrats on the committee pressed Mukasey on whether he considered waterboarding—a technique that simulates drowning, which the CIA had used on high-value terror suspects post-9/11—to be illegal torture under U.S. and international law.

Mukasey refused to explicitly classify waterboarding as torture. 

While he stated that waterboarding was "repugnant" and that "if waterboarding is torture, it is illegal," he declined to definitively label it as such. Mukasey argued that as an outsider not currently privy to the classified details of the CIA’s actual interrogation techniques, he could not make a legal determination. Furthermore, he expressed concern that declaring the technique illegal could expose U.S. intelligence officials who had previously used it to criminal prosecution or civil liability.

His refusal ignited an uproar among human rights advocates and Congressional Democrats, who argued that waterboarding had been recognized as torture since the Spanish Inquisition and had been prosecuted as a war crime by the United States following World War II.

---

### The Senate Divide and Committee Drama

The revelation turned Mukasey’s confirmation into a referendum on the Bush administration’s counterterrorism policies and the legal boundaries of executive authority. 

Democrats, led by Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy (D-VT), argued that an Attorney General must be willing to place clear legal limits on executive power. Leahy and several high-profile Democrats announced their intention to vote against Mukasey, demanding that he unequivocally declare waterboarding illegal before receiving their support.

The debate forced key Democratic senators into a political dilemma. On one hand, voting against Mukasey risked leaving the Department of Justice without a confirmed leader during a critical time. On the other, voting for him was seen by critics as a tacit endorsement of "enhanced interrogation techniques."

The breakthrough for the Bush administration came from two key Democratic members of the Judiciary Committee: Senators **Chuck Schumer** (D-NY) and **Dianne Feinstein** (D-CA). Both expressed deep disappointment with Mukasey’s answers on torture, but both ultimately decided that having a strong, independent Attorney General was preferable to leaving the department in the hands of an acting official accountable only to the White House.

On November 6, 2007, the Judiciary Committee approved Mukasey’s nomination by an **11–9 vote**, sending it to the full Senate floor. Schumer and Feinstein were the only Democrats to vote "yes."

---

### The Confirmation Vote Tallies

On November 8, 2007, the full United States Senate voted on the confirmation of Michael Mukasey as the 81st Attorney General of the United States. 

The final vote was **53 to 40**, marking one of the narrowest confirmation margins for an Attorney General in modern U.S. history. 

#### **The Breakdown of the Senate Vote:**
* **Republicans:** Voted unanimously in favor (46 YES votes).
* **Democrats:** The vast majority voted against confirmation. Only six Democrats crossed party lines to join Republicans in voting YES:
  * Chuck Schumer (NY)
  * Dianne Feinstein (CA)
  * Evan Bayh (IN)
  * Thomas Carper (DE)
  * Mary Landrieu (LA)
  * Ben Nelson (NE)
* **Independents:** Joe Lieberman (CT) voted YES, while Bernie Sanders (VT) voted NO.
* **Absentees:** Seven senators did not vote, largely due to commitments on the 2008 presidential campaign trail.

#### **Impact of the 2008 Presidential Election:**
The vote took place in the shadow of the upcoming 2008 presidential race, transforming the confirmation into a key campaign issue:
* Democratic presidential candidates **Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton, and Joe Biden** all strongly opposed Mukasey's nomination over the waterboarding issue (though Obama and Clinton missed the final floor vote due to campaigning, both stated publicly they opposed him).
* Republican nominee **John McCain**—himself a survivor of torture as a prisoner of war in Vietnam and a vocal opponent of waterboarding—ultimately voted **YES** to confirm Mukasey, arguing the Department of Justice urgently needed a confirmed leader, though he publicly maintained that waterboarding was indisputably torture.

---

### Public Opinion and Polling Dynamics

The Senate vote mirrored a broader, deeply polarized public debate regarding enhanced interrogation tactics in the post-9/11 era.

During late 2007, national public opinion polls reflected a conflicted American electorate:

1. **Split on Waterboarding:** Gallup and Pew Research polls from the 2005–2007 era showed that the American public was roughly divided on harsh interrogation tactics. When asked abstractly about "torture," a vast majority of Americans opposed it. However, when polls framed the question around using "harsh interrogation techniques" on suspected terrorists to prevent future attacks, public support often hovered between 40% and 50%.
2. **Partisan Polarization:** Polling highlighted a massive partisan divide. A majority of self-identified Republicans viewed techniques like waterboarding as necessary tools for national security, while a vast majority of Democrats viewed them as illegal and immoral practices that damaged America's standing in the world.
3. **Approval of the DOJ:** At the time of the vote, public trust in the Department of Justice was at a historic low due to the scandals surrounding Alberto Gonzales. While polling indicated that the public wanted a non-partisan figure to restore trust to the DOJ, Mukasey’s testimony ensured that his confirmation would be evaluated through the lens of executive power rather than judicial neutrality.

---

### Legacy and Aftermath

Michael Mukasey was sworn in as Attorney General on November 9, 2007, and served through the end of the Bush administration in January 2009. 

During his tenure, Mukasey maintained his stance that he would not prosecute CIA officers who had engaged in waterboarding, as they were acting in good faith based on legal memorandums provided by the Justice Department at the time (the so-called "Torture Memos").

The controversy surrounding his confirmation vote presaged the official end of the policy. Just two days after taking office in January 2009, President Barack Obama signed Executive Order 13491, officially banning waterboarding and limiting U.S. personnel to interrogation techniques outlined in the Army Field Manual.

The narrow 53–40 vote confirming Mukasey stands as a historical marker—a snapshot of a nation and a legislature deeply divided over the legal, moral, and national security implications of the War on Terror.
